findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Mild aortic valve sclerosis without stenosis. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
echo.impression: Structurally normal heart apart from mild aortic valve sclerosis without stenosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral Hoover sign, give-way weakness that becomes full with distraction, a gait that normalizes when unobserved, and an observed event of shaking while talking then motionless unresponsiveness with recall
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe the events
action_criteria.rationale: His limb weakness and his events are diagnosed by positive features (DSM-5 criterion B), and the examination separates them from the signs of his known diabetic neuropathy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Eosinophils 0.82 with ESR 28 and CRP 8.4 mg/L: mild systemic activity on a steroid taper, which says nothing specific about the brain
action_criteria.label: Check blood count with eosinophils, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: The referring team suspected vasculitic seizures: eosinophils and inflammatory markers show how active the systemic vasculitis is on the prednisolone taper, which the rheumatology plan needs.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Only punctate small vessel white matter hyperintensities up to 4 mm, with no infarct, microhemorrhage or inflammatory lesion to suggest CNS vasculitis
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast for the CNS vasculitis question
action_criteria.rationale: New events at 62 in a man with eosinophilic vasculitis, who fears cerebral spread and whose referring team suspected vasculitic seizures: one non-contrast MRI with DWI, FLAIR and SWI answers that specific question once.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record both types of habitual event on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: Late-onset daily events that did not respond to levetiracetam or diazepam: recording both the shaking and the unresponsive events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level and gives the strongest basis for withdrawing both drugs (AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam and diazepam to withdraw gradually, sedation and falls with tamsulosin, mood effects shared with prednisolone, and steroid-raised glucose on metformin
action_criteria.label: Review the antiseizure drug and benzodiazepine before withdrawal
action_criteria.rationale: Levetiracetam and diazepam were started for misdiagnosed events and are to be withdrawn; their interactions with his prednisolone, tamsulosin and diabetes treatment shape the plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies comorbid mood, anxiety and dissociation with performance-validity measures to plan treatment; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment
action_criteria.rationale: A battery would quantify his health anxiety, grief and caregiver strain for the treatment plan, but it does not make the diagnosis, which rests on the examination, and it is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on positive diagnosis and on physiotherapy and psychological therapy for FND; no step of this patient's work-up depends on it
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: A literature search is background reading, not a clinical step in this patient's pathway; no step of the work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures, or stop it abruptly.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
Treat the events as CNS vasculitis with high-dose corticosteroids or cyclophosphamide.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional seizures, with functional limb weakness) based on the semiology of the two types of habitual event (speech preserved during bilateral shaking, a motionless phase with recall), confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and the Hoover sign, collapsing weakness and distractibility, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid health anxiety about his vasculitis, with his grief and caregiver strain.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

Taper and stop levetiracetam, then diazepam, under neurological supervision, one drug at a time, once the events are securely diagnosed as functional (ideally with a habitual event documented on video-EEG) and there is no evidence of epilepsy.
Continue the treatment of the eosinophilic vasculitis, including the prednisolone taper, with rheumatology.

avoided_actions.rationale: No structural cardiac question: vital signs stay normal during events and awareness is preserved.
Telemetry at the referring hospital showed no arrhythmia during witnessed events, and the events are recorded on video-EEG; further rhythm monitoring answers no question.
A CT adds nothing to the brain MRI that answers the vasculitis question.
FDG-PET has no role: the events have no ictal correlate and the MRI shows no inflammatory lesion.
His diabetic neuropathy is already established and the give-way weakness becomes full with distraction; EMG and nerve conduction answer no question about the events.
His arm sensory loss with a sharp cutoff at the shoulder is not a somatosensory pathway question; evoked potentials add nothing.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder - psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) with dissociative episodes, in the context of eosinophilic vasculitis (EGPA), bereavement, and health anxiety

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. Speech during bilateral shaking and a motionless phase with recall do not fit epileptic seizures.

The vasculitis and raised eosinophils, ESR and CRP raise the question, but the brain MRI shows only small vessel change with no infarct or microhemorrhage, there is no focal deficit or encephalopathy, and the events have no ictal change.
He reports palpitations, but telemetry showed no arrhythmia during events, vital signs stay stable, and he talks during the shaking.

differential.diagnosis: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy as the cause of the weakness
differential.key_features: Stocking pinprick and vibration loss, reduced reflexes and absent ankle jerks are those of his known neuropathy; proximal give-way weakness that becomes full with distraction is not.

key_clinical_evidence: Seven habitual events of two types (shaking with preserved speech, and motionless unresponsiveness with recall) were recorded on 4-day video-EEG without ictal change.
Positive signs of functional weakness: Hoover sign on both sides, collapsing weakness, distractibility and a gait that normalizes when unobserved.
The non-contrast brain MRI shows only small vessel change, with no lesion of CNS vasculitis; raised eosinophils, ESR and CRP reflect the systemic disease.
Levetiracetam and diazepam, started for the events without benefit, are to be withdrawn one at a time; the vasculitis treatment continues.
Bereavement, caregiver strain and fear that the vasculitis has reached the brain are context and treatment targets, not the basis of the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A systemic vasculitis raises the question of CNS involvement, but the MRI shows no vasculitic lesion and the recorded events have no ictal change.
red_herrings.data_point: Eosinophilic vasculitis, with the referring team suspecting vasculitis-related seizures
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the events to CNS vasculitis and escalate immunosuppression

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Eosinophilia and mildly raised ESR and CRP reflect the systemic vasculitis on a steroid taper and say nothing specific about the brain.
red_herrings.data_point: Eosinophils 0.82 x10^9/L, ESR 28 mm/hr, CRP 8.4 mg/L
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the inflammatory markers as evidence of CNS vasculitis and pursue lumbar puncture or angiography

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Punctate periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities at 62 with diabetes and hypertension are small vessel change, not vasculitis.
red_herrings.data_point: Scattered punctate white matter hyperintensities, largest 4 mm, on brain MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: Read the white matter change as CNS vasculitis

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A paternal aunt with childhood-onset epilepsy does not make late-onset events epileptic; the recorded events without ictal change show they are not.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic cause and continue levetiracetam

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A remote anxiety disorder and recent bereavement neither establish nor refute FND; they are treatment targets.
red_herrings.data_point: Anxiety disorder in his 40s, death of his wife 18 months ago and caregiving for his mother
red_herrings.intended_effect: Label the events psychological without positive evidence, or dismiss FND because he is 'just anxious'

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: Hip extension weak on direct testing on each side, full during flexion of the opposite hip against resistance.
Left deltoid, both biceps and both hip flexors start at 4/5 and collapse suddenly against resistance, then return to 5/5 on repeat testing.
Full 5/5 strength with distraction; Romberg swaying lessens when distracted by conversation.
Lurching gait with wide swaying improves to a fluent normal gait when he walks to the bathroom unaware of being observed.
Reflexes 1+ in the arms and at the knees, ankle jerks absent, plantar responses flexor; stocking loss of pinprick and vibration below mid-calf.
Loss of light touch over the whole left arm with a sharp cutoff at the shoulder; not counted as a rule-in sign.

A 15-second episode of facial grimacing and irregular shaking of all four limbs while he kept talking, followed by 90 seconds of unresponsiveness with eyes closed, during which a dropped hand was deflected from his face; he recalled the whole episode and had no confusion.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: Hoover sign on both sides, collapsing weakness, distractibility and inconsistency between examination and function. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (bilateral shaking with preserved speech, a motionless unresponsive phase with closed eyes and recall, no confusion) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Prednisolone with metformin: corticosteroids raise blood glucose and oppose the glucose-lowering effect; monitor glucose, more closely at higher steroid doses.
Diazepam with tamsulosin: additive dizziness and orthostatic hypotension from sedation and alpha-blockade; risk of falls.
Diazepam with levetiracetam: additive central nervous system depression (somnolence, unsteadiness).
No other clinically significant interaction among the current medicines.
general.proposed: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily; Lisinopril 10 mg once daily; Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily; Diazepam 2 mg as needed up to three times daily; Prednisolone 15 mg once daily, tapering course; Tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily
general.summary: Prednisolone raises glucose against metformin; diazepam adds sedation and fall risk with levetiracetam and tamsulosin; levetiracetam and prednisolone can both worsen anxiety and mood; withdraw the antiseizure drug and benzodiazepine gradually.
warnings: Levetiracetam: psychiatric and behavioral adverse effects (irritability, anxiety, low mood); withdraw by gradual dose reduction rather than abruptly.
Diazepam: as-needed use for a short period carries a low dependence risk; avoid abrupt cessation after regular use.
Prednisolone: insomnia, anxiety and mood change are common adverse effects; hyperglycemia in diabetes.

artifacts.impact: Moderate artifact during shaking episodes, but underlying cerebral activity clearly identifiable in posterior leads where persistent alpha rhythm is visible throughout all events

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 9.5 Hz alpha rhythm, symmetric, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture with vertex waves, K-complexes, and sleep spindles. All sleep stages recorded. No interictal epileptiform discharges during sleep.

findings.frequency: Four events over 4 days; durations 15, 30, 22 and 40 seconds
findings.morphology: During all four events, the EEG showed persistent normal waking alpha rhythm with superimposed muscle and movement artifact. No ictal pattern, no rhythmic evolution, no electrodecrement, no post-event slowing. Video: facial grimacing, then bilateral lower limb tremor progressing to irregular shaking of all extremities, waxing and waning and varying between events. The patient talks during the events and in one says 'I can feel it happening' while the background is normal. No tongue biting or incontinence; transient toe discoloration on video.
findings.type: Clinical events, type 1: shaking of all four limbs

findings.morphology: Normal waking EEG with reactive posterior alpha rhythm persisted throughout all three episodes. No slowing, no electrodecrement, no focal or generalized rhythmic activity. Video: patient lies motionless with eyes closed, not responding to voice or touch. In one event, a hand dropped above his face was deflected away from it; in another, brief eyelid flutter followed a loud call of his name. Afterwards he states he was aware throughout but unable to move or speak.
Low-amplitude 18-25 Hz fast activity, diffuse and symmetric; a nonspecific finding.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Seven habitual events were recorded (four episodes of irregular shaking of all four limbs with preserved speech, 15 to 40 seconds, and three episodes of motionless unresponsiveness with eyes closed, 75 to 120 seconds) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures. Mild diffuse excess beta activity is nonspecific.
eeg.limitations: None significant. Adequate number of habitual events of both types captured. Diazepam was not tapered during monitoring given the low dose and short duration of use.

labs.interpretation: Eosinophilia (0.82 x10^9/L). Raised ESR (28 mm/hr) and CRP (8.4 mg/L). Glucose 148 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.8% (high). Mildly raised AST (42 U/L) and ALT (58 U/L). Remaining values within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

additional_observations: Technique: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and SWI, without contrast.
No infarct of any age, focal edema or hemorrhage
Normal vascular flow voids in major intracranial arteries
Bilateral ethmoid sinus mucosal thickening is an incidental finding

signal_characteristics.FLAIR: No cortical or deep gray matter signal abnormality
signal_characteristics.SWI: No microhemorrhage or other susceptibility abnormality

findings.location: Bilateral periventricular and deep white matter, predominantly frontal

mri.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. Scattered punctate periventricular and deep white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, largest 4 mm, without restricted diffusion, consistent with chronic small vessel ischemic change. No infarct, hemorrhage, microhemorrhage or mass. Incidental mild ethmoid mucosal thickening.

metadata.condition_name: Functional neurological disorder - Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) with dissociative episodes
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: a coexisting eosinophilic vasculitis with raised eosinophils, ESR and CRP anchors on cerebral vasculitis, white matter change on MRI and palpitations add misdirection, and the age and sex are atypical for FND; the event semiology and the positive signs make the diagnosis, and two drugs must be withdrawn.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional seizures with functional limb weakness and an organic comorbidity: the examination and the event semiology make the diagnosis, with video-EEG confirmation if recorded, a single non-contrast MRI and inflammatory markers answer the vasculitis question, and the medication review plans the withdrawal.
metadata.estimated_complexity: Diagnostic puzzle: a systemic autoimmune disease with abnormal inflammatory markers and white matter change invites a vasculitic explanation of functional seizures and functional weakness in an older man.
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: policy tiers, reports and assessment rebuilt to the FND condition plan. Close-out 24 Oct 2026: video-EEG optional and red-flag tests recommended, per the July 2026 agreement with the physicians that the examination is the only required diagnostic act.
metadata.sub_domain: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures with systemic autoimmune anchoring

patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent seizure-like episodes with limb shaking and periods of unresponsiveness for 4 weeks, unresponsive to levetiracetam and diazepam

family_history: Father died of myocardial infarction at age 71
Mother had type 2 diabetes and dementia (onset in her 80s)
One brother (age 65) with essential tremor diagnosed at age 58
One sister (age 57) with fibromyalgia and depression

medications.indication: Seizure-like episodes (started 3 weeks ago by referring physician)

medications.frequency: As needed up to three times daily

past_medical_history: Eosinophilic vasculitis diagnosed 3 months ago, treated with methotrexate (discontinued 2 weeks prior to transfer due to elevated liver enzymes)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at age 52, with peripheral neuropathy (distal symmetric sensorimotor)
Prior retinal detachment of the left eye requiring surgery at age 55
Remote history of anxiety disorder in his 40s, treated briefly with counseling, no pharmacotherapy

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, approximately 2-3 units per week. Denies recent increase.
social_history.exercise: Previously walked daily, now minimal due to episodes and fear of falling
social_history.living_situation: Lives alone following the death of his wife 18 months ago from breast cancer. Provides regular caregiving assistance to his 88-year-old mother who lives nearby and has mild cognitive impairment. His adult son lives abroad.
social_history.occupation: Retired civil engineer, stopped working at age 60 due to declining health
social_history.psychosocial_stressors: Wife died 18 months ago after prolonged illness. Patient describes intense grief and difficulty adjusting to living alone. He has taken on caregiving responsibilities for his elderly mother, which he finds physically and emotionally exhausting. Recent diagnosis of eosinophilic vasculitis caused significant health anxiety, particularly concerns about long-term prognosis and immunosuppression during the COVID-19 pandemic. He reports feeling overwhelmed and describes a sense of losing control over his health.
social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 15 pack-year history, quit at age 50

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Harrington is a 62-year-old right-handed Caucasian man transferred from a regional hospital to the neurology service for further evaluation of recurrent paroxysmal episodes that began approximately four weeks ago. These episodes were initially attributed to possible epileptic seizures in the context of his recently diagnosed eosinophilic vasculitis, raising concerns for cerebral vasculitis-related seizures.

The episodes typically begin with a pulsating or whooshing sensation in both ears, followed by a wave of tension and aching pain that radiates down his limbs. This prodromal phase lasts 10-20 seconds before progressing to visible facial grimacing and bilateral lower extremity tremor that can escalate to violent shaking of all four limbs. The movements are irregular, waxing and waning in intensity, and each shaking episode lasts between 10 and 45 seconds. The patient reports remaining fully conscious and aware throughout the motor phase and can describe what is happening in real time. He denies any loss of consciousness, tongue biting, or urinary or bladder incontinence during any episode.

Following the motor phase, he enters a period of apparent unresponsiveness lasting one to three minutes during which he lies still with his eyes closed. He reports being fully aware during these periods but states he is unable to move or speak. Staff report that his vital signs remain entirely stable throughout, with normal oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure during and after events. He also describes palpitations associated with the episodes, though continuous telemetry at the referring hospital showed no arrhythmias during witnessed events.

Notably, his toes develop transient peripheral cyanosis during episodes, which the referring team attributed to his vasculitis. The episodes occur two to four times daily and are almost exclusively witnessed by nursing staff or family, rarely occurring when the patient is alone. The episodes have been refractory to a trial of levetiracetam (500 mg twice daily for three weeks) and low-dose diazepam (2 mg as needed), which were started empirically at the referring hospital.

The patient is significantly distressed about these episodes and expresses recurrent fears that his vasculitis has spread to his brain. He lost his wife to breast cancer eighteen months ago and has been struggling with bereavement, social isolation, and the dual burden of managing his own new diagnosis while caring for his elderly mother. He reports poor sleep, reduced appetite, and a pervasive feeling of losing control over his body since the vasculitis diagnosis.

neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, one episode was witnessed in two phases. First, the patient reported a pulsating sensation in his ears, then developed facial grimacing and rhythmic tremor of both lower limbs progressing to violent shaking of all extremities lasting approximately 15 seconds. He remained conversant throughout, stating 'it's happening again.' No tongue biting, no incontinence. Oxygen saturation remained 98% and heart rate 76 bpm during the event. Second, following the shaking, he became unresponsive for approximately 90 seconds with eyes closed, not responding to verbal commands or sternal rub. When his hand was held above his face and dropped, he deflected it away from his face. On recovery, he stated he had been fully aware throughout but could not move or speak. No post-ictal confusion. The toes developed transient peripheral cyanosis (Raynaud-like). Staff noted that events occurred almost exclusively in the presence of observers.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Left eye with surgical changes from prior retinal detachment repair (mild visual acuity reduction OS, 20/30). Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient walks with an unusual lurching pattern with excessive swaying side to side but does not fall. When observed walking to the bathroom while he believes he is unobserved, gait is significantly more fluent and normal. Tandem gait performed with dramatic difficulty, arms widely abducted, but no actual falls. Romberg test: marked swaying with eyes closed but improves when distracted by conversation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Affect is anxious, with frequent sighing. Speech is fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Attention: digit span 6 forward, 4 backward. Memory 3/3 registration, 3/3 recall at 5 minutes. Clock drawing test normal (10/10). No thought disorder. Patient becomes visibly distressed when discussing his episodes and repeatedly asks whether he could have cerebral vasculitis.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk throughout. Tone normal, no rigidity or spasticity. Upper extremities: inconsistent 'give-way' weakness noted on left deltoid and bilateral biceps flexion testing: strength appears 4/5 initially but collapses suddenly against resistance, then returns to 5/5 on repeat testing. With encouragement and distraction, full 5/5 strength is consistently demonstrated. Lower extremities: similar inconsistent give-way pattern in bilateral hip flexors, less prominent in knee extensors. No pronator drift. No atrophy or fasciculations. Hoover sign positive bilaterally: hip extension is weak on direct testing on each side but full during flexion of the opposite hip against resistance.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 1+ at biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis bilaterally (globally hyporeflexic). 1+ at patellae bilaterally. Ankle jerks absent bilaterally (consistent with diabetic neuropathy). Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus. No Hoffman sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact in upper extremities. Reduced pinprick and vibration sense in a stocking distribution below the mid-calf bilaterally, consistent with known diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Proprioception intact at the great toes bilaterally. No dermatomal sensory loss. Reported loss of light touch over the entire left arm with a sharp circumferential cutoff at the shoulder, which does not conform to any peripheral nerve, root or vascular territory.
